findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 – External Auditors Annual Report (VfM) for the year ended 31 March 2026
findings.headline: The 2026/27 budget includes £230k of premises efficiency savings, with no consolidated schedule of individual measures, delivery status or ownership.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 – External Auditors Annual Report (VfM) for the year ended 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Capital programme delivery was 69% in 2024/25 and 48% in 2025/26, with £2.619m carried forward into 2026/27.
findings.detail: The auditor says repeated slippage shows planned delivery timescales have been too optimistic, and that the delays had project-specific causes rather than a single control failure. The 2025/26 programme was £5.044m with £2.430m spent or committed.
findings.matters: Two consecutive years of under-delivery, with carry-forward growing into the final budget year, is the pattern a finance director would check when assessing a council's capital plan.
findings.quote: The Council delivered 69% of its capital programme in 2024/25 and 48% in 2025/26, with £2.619m carried forward into 2026/27.

findings.headline: The General Fund working balance was £1.555m at 31 March 2026, against a £1.5m minimum.

findings.matters: Full delivery of a savings target in a year of overspend shows the savings programme landing as planned, which peer finance teams with similar targets will compare against.

findings.matters: A completed scheme landing £50,000 under budget with a 25-year warranty is a delivery outcome a finance director can compare against their own roofing and building programmes.

findings.matters: A scheme delivered under its budget after an estimate-driven delay and a supplementary funding request shows one route through a budget gap that other councils may recognise.

findings.matters: Tender prices above budget on a building with a structural constraint, requiring approval from both the existing council and the shadow authority, is a cost pressure other councils with local government reorganisation underway may face.

findings.headline: Bourne Hall Replacement Heating & Ventilation has a £1,000,000 budget and a £60,000 year-end forecast, with further funding required before the next stages.
findings.detail: Surveys on ducting and asbestos are still under way, and consultants have offered two options: works in occupation, which are much higher cost and take considerably longer, or works with the building shut. The manager says further funding is required to proceed to the next stages if the in-occupation option is chosen.
findings.matters: A £1m scheme that now forecasts £60,000 spend this year, with a funding request still to be made, shows the scale of capital reprofiling a finance director may need to manage.

findings.detail: The fee excludes the separate Housing Benefit audit. The report says the £3,000 uplift relates to additional work on IFRIC 14 pensions accounting and is provided for within existing budgets.
findings.matters: The uplift is attributed to IFRIC 14 pensions work, which other councils with defined benefit schemes may also face when auditors review surplus and minimum funding requirements.

findings.detail: The report lists three areas for improvement identified in the audit. The Audit Findings Report sets out recommendations and management actions on these points, which the committee is asked to note.
findings.matters: Collection Fund reporting and year-end close controls are common audit pressure points across English councils, so the named areas are useful for peers reviewing their own controls.
findings.quote: mainly around Collection Fund reporting, year-end accounts preparation and review, and HR/new starter controls.

findings.headline: The number of value for money recommendations from the external auditor is now two, after what the report describes as progress over the last three years.

findings.matters: The trend in auditor value for money findings is a direct indicator of governance quality that finance directors at other councils can benchmark against.

findings.headline: Grant Thornton anticipates an unmodified (clean) opinion on Epsom and Ewell's 2025/26 financial statements, subject to a few outstanding items.

findings.matters: A clean opinion on the accounts is the baseline assurance a lender or peer finance director looks for, and this paper reports it as anticipated rather than final.
findings.quote: the auditors anticipate issuing an unmodified (clean) opinion on the financial statements.

findings.headline: Management did not account for £111k of annual holiday accruals at 31 March 2026, and the amount is left unadjusted in the financial statements.

Management's stated reason is that the amount is immaterial. The schedule's overall impact is £111k on the comprehensive income and expenditure statement, the balance sheet, and the general fund.
findings.matters: Leave accruals are a routine year-end adjustment, so a finance officer at another council can compare how this council handled the same item and where it set its materiality threshold.

findings.headline: Housing Services recorded 151 successful interventions in Q2 2026/27, and 325 across Q1 and Q2 combined.
findings.detail: The Q2 total includes 21 cases where homelessness was prevented or relieved under statutory duties and 130 cases where homelessness was prevented through early intervention. The paper presents these as evidence of the prevention strategy's success.
findings.matters: A council that can show prevention outcomes against rising demand is giving its finance team evidence that spending on early intervention is reducing the number of costly placements.

findings.headline: 142 households were in nightly paid accommodation at the end of September 2026.
findings.detail: The paper says this increase, and the rise in homeless approaches, is largely attributable to friends and family eviction, private rented sector pressures and households fleeing violence. It gives no cost figure for nightly paid accommodation in this extract.
findings.matters: Nightly paid accommodation is typically the most expensive form of temporary housing, so the household count is a key input for any finance officer estimating the cost of temporary accommodation.
findings.figures: 142 households in nightly paid accommodation at end September
findings.quote: The number of households in nightly paid accommodation at end September was 142.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation demand rose 21% in the first two quarters of 2026/27 compared with the same period of 2025/26.
findings.detail: The paper links the increase to friends and family evictions, private rented sector pressures and households fleeing violence. It sets this 21% rise against the 39% rise in applications and presents the gap as showing the prevention and move-on strategy is working.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation demand is a recurring cost pressure for councils, so a comparison of demand growth with application growth is relevant to any council planning for it.
findings.figures: 21% increase in demand for temporary accommodation; 39% increase in homelessness applications
findings.quote: 2026/27, by 21% compared to the same period in 2025/26.

findings.headline: Homelessness applications were up 39% in Q1 and Q2 2026/27 compared with the same quarters of 2025/26, with 382 applications received.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the rise to friends and family evictions, pressures in the private rented sector and households fleeing violence, alongside a chronic shortage of affordable housing and limited move-on options. It reports the increase as a demand figure and does not give a cost.
findings.matters: Rising homelessness approaches are the upstream driver of temporary accommodation demand, which a finance director would need to track against budget.
findings.figures: 39% increase in homelessness applications in Q1&2; 382 applications received
findings.quote: quarters in 2025/26, with a total of 382 applications received.

findings.headline: Council says Local Government Reorganisation introduces uncertainty that may change funding, asset ownership and delivery responsibilities for capital schemes
findings.detail: The paper says LGR could affect the viability, scope and timing of schemes in development or delivery. Officers will review the programme against LGR to ensure commitments remain appropriate and deliverable.
findings.matters: Reorganisation of council structures that could move capital assets and funding is a risk that finance directors and lenders would need to price into any multi-year capital plan.
findings.figures: None quantified in the paper
findings.quote: LGR introduces a significant degree of uncertainty and transition risk that must be carefully considered in the management of the Council’s capital programme.

findings.detail: The paper says the increases are likely to affect both current and future capital projects, and it links the risk to the Council's ability to source contractors within budget.
findings.matters: Contractor tender pressure from inflation is a cost risk that a finance director would expect to see in forecasts and that peers facing similar tender markets would compare against.
findings.figures: None quantified in the paper
findings.quote: Global events and rising inflation have caused firms to significantly increase their quotes for works, having a major impact on the Council’s ability to source contractors within budget.

findings.matters: A scheme whose cost and completion date both move during the year is the kind of project slippage a finance director and peer councils would track.

findings.matters: A reserve drawn down to fund capital, then partly rebuilt by a single asset sale, is the funding position a finance director and lender would track to judge future borrowing need.

findings.matters: A council stating that reorganisation could change its funding and service responsibilities is relevant to lenders and to finance officers at other councils facing the same process.

findings.quote: Nevertheless, there is concern that homelessness numbers will remain high and possibly rise still further, particularly with the onset of winter, which historically sees increased demand.

findings.headline: No new affordable housing was delivered in the past year, constraining the council's ability to move people on from temporary accommodation
findings.detail: The paper identifies lack of newly developed affordable housing as a root cause, noting zero units were delivered in the past year. With the private rental sector also unaffordable, this creates a structural constraint that may persist despite increased spending.
findings.matters: This identifies an underlying supply-side constraint that spending more on temporary accommodation services alone cannot solve. The problem may be structural, not operational.
findings.figures: No new affordable housing units delivered in past year
findings.quote: The review of service delivery , highlights that without access to sufficient affordable accommodation, and with much of the private rental sector remaining unaffordable, temporary accommodation (TA) usage may increase further.

findings.headline: Council is allocating £750k growth budget and £128.5k in-year funding to temporary accommodation to address a structural deficit
findings.detail: The council is allocating £750k in growth funding for 2026/27 and an additional £128.5k in-year to temporary accommodation. The paper describes this as addressing a structural deficit in the service.
findings.matters: The scale of allocation shows the council recognizes this as a major problem and is taking action to manage it, but also signals the problem is substantial and structural.
findings.figures: £750k growth budget for 2026/27; £128.5k in-year increase
findings.quote: It is worth noting that £750k growth budget was put into the nightly paid service for 2026/27 to address some of the structural deficit in this area . Furthermore, the budget has been further increased by £128.5k in year, funded from the inflationary provision.

findings.headline: Homelessness applications have surged 86% in two years, with nightly paid accommodation numbers rising from approximately 20 to approximately 120
findings.detail: The paper shows homeless households in nightly paid accommodation rising from approximately 20 in April 2022 to approximately 120 by June 2026. Homelessness applications have risen each year, with recent years showing particularly steep increases.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess whether this demand-driven growth is unsustainable or cyclical, and whether the council can continue to fund it. Demand has roughly doubled in 2 years.
findings.figures: 86% rise in homelessness applications over two years; nightly paid accommodation rising from approximately 20 to approximately 120
findings.quote: The tables below show the total number of homeless households in nightly paid accommodation over the past four years and the huge rise (86%) in homelessness applications over the past two years.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation service shows £0.250m adverse variance in Q1 2026 due to elevated numbers of homeless households
findings.detail: The first-quarter forecast shows a £0.250m overspend in temporary accommodation. This is driven by higher than expected numbers of homeless households requiring nightly paid accommodation.
findings.matters: A material overspend in a demand-driven social care service that the council is legally obliged to fund, and one that continues to grow.
findings.figures: £ 0.250m adverse variance
findings.quote: The updated forecast for  end June 2026 is a net adverse variance of £ 0.250m, due to the continued elevated numbers of households in temporary accommodation (TA).

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation flagged as presenting significant uncertainty and transition risk to funding and budget assumptions
findings.detail: The paper states LGR 'must be actively considered throughout the Council's revenue budget monitoring process' and warns that 'potential changes to funding streams, service delivery responsibilities, and strategic priorities may emerge' which 'could directly influence the assumptions underpinning the revenue budget.'
findings.matters: Lenders need assurance that a council's funding model and service base are stable; LGR creates material uncertainty around future funding levels and service delivery that could affect financial capacity.
findings.figures: None quantified
findings.quote: Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) presents a significant degree of uncertainty and transition risk, which must be actively considered throughout the Council's revenue budget monitoring process.

findings.headline: Budget relies on £1.38m (11.6% of total) dividend income from commercial property company EEPIC; no performance data disclosed
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget includes £1.38m dividend income from Epsom and Ewell Property Investment Company, representing 11.6% of the £11.868m revenue budget. The paper provides no information on EEPIC's property performance, occupancy, or risk of dividend reduction. Combined with housing contingency already consumed in Q1, the budget has little buffer if dividend income falls.
findings.matters: Revenue budgets dependent on commercial property dividends face significant volatility; a decline in property values or rental income could turn a balanced budget into a deficit.
findings.figures: £1.38m dividend income; £11.868m total budget
findings.quote: The Council's 2026/27 budget includes £1.38m expected dividend income from Epsom and Ewell Property Investment Company, generated from its two commercial properties.

findings.headline: Revenue reserves forecast to fall 21% year-on-year, with general-purpose reserves declining 37% from £4.9m to £3.1m
findings.detail: Total reserves fall from £19.954m (April 2026) to £15.650m (March 2027), a £4.3m reduction. More significantly, reserves available for general use decline from £4.863m to £3.050m—a 37% fall in the council's financial buffer. This is driven by planned drawdown of earmarked reserves (£763k) and contingency allocation to cover housing overspend.
findings.matters: Sharp reserve depletion in a single year weakens a council's financial resilience and capacity to absorb future shocks; a 37% decline signals tightening headroom for unplanned pressures.
findings.figures: Total reserves £19.954m to £15.650m; general-use reserves £4.863m to £3.050m

findings.headline: Housing overspend of £250k in Q1 despite increasing nightly accommodation budget to 100 households, driven by Renters Rights Act evictions
findings.detail: The council increased its homelessness budget for 2026/27 to accommodate 100 households in nightly paid accommodation, but demand surged further in Q1 as landlords responded to the May implementation of the Renters Rights Act. The resulting £250k overspend is covered by corporate contingency. The Section 151 Officer notes the position remains 'highly sensitive to fluctuations in demand, availability of accommodation and wider housing market conditions.'
findings.matters: Demand-driven overspends in statutory services signal budget control weakness; with contingency already allocated in Q1, further demand growth would force service cuts or reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: £250k adverse variance; budgeted for 100 households; total budget £11.868m
findings.quote: Despite t he substantial increase in the Council's nightly paid accommodation budget for 2026/27, increased to accommodate an average of 100 households in nightly paid accommodation, demand has dramatically increased in the first quarter as landlords responded to the implementation of the Renters Rights Act  in May.

findings.headline: Audit weakness in governance arrangement transparency identified in 2023/24 but addressed and closed by 2024/25
findings.detail: In February 2025, Grant Thornton identified a significant weakness in governance arrangements; the council had made changes but did not promptly inform auditors. The council subsequently updated its constitution, clarified delegation frameworks, and established regular engagement with auditors. By February 2026, auditors confirmed these improvements had addressed the prior weakness with no new weaknesses identified.
findings.matters: Audit weaknesses are material to lender assessment of governance quality; this paper shows a weakness was promptly identified and resolved with auditor confirmation.
findings.figures: Weakness identified in 2023/24 audit (reported February 2025); addressed by 2024/25 audit (reported February 2026)
findings.quote: The LGA Peer Review also identified the need for a more transparent approach. We note that the Council has since updated its constitution, clarified delegation frameworks, and maintained regular and open engagement with audit, thereby addressing and closing the prior year's key recommendation.

findings.headline: £1 million Bourne Hall heating and ventilation scheme in early design stage; asbestos survey and listed building consent still pending.
findings.detail: This major scheme has only £60,000 forecast spend (6% of budget). The council must complete asbestos and ventilation plant surveys before listed building consent can be sought or tenders issued. Key decisions about building closure during works remain unmade.
findings.matters: Large project with significant delivery uncertainty; asbestos survey and listed building consent requirements create material risk of delay and cost increases.
findings.figures: Budget £1,000,000, Year end forecast £60,000, Variance (£940,000), Actuals to Q1 £0
findings.quote: Design work has commenced and some initial proposals discussed with EEBC. Awaiting further surveys on ventilation plant and asbestos before we can apply for listed building consent or send out to tender. Some decisions are to be made on whether we shut the building to carry out the works.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation modular units project on hold due to legal challenge; procurement delayed to October 2026 with completion date uncertain.
findings.detail: Three modular family units (planning approved November 2024) have been held up by a legal challenge. A project manager was recently appointed. Procurement is unlikely to start before October 2026, and completion is now listed as 'To be advised'. The £411,036 budget has been carried forward from 2024/25.
findings.matters: Shows execution risk on housing investment. Extended delay from legal challenge and slow procurement restart indicates housing delivery pressure.
findings.figures: Budget £411,036 (carried from 2024/25), Year end forecast £411,036, Actuals to Q1 £2,013
findings.quote: The project had been on hold due to a legal challenge. A project manager is now on board. The Procurement process is unlikely to start before October 2026.

findings.headline: Wellbeing Centre windows replacement and solar panel installation projects deferred indefinitely due to Local Government Reorganisation uncertainty.
findings.detail: Two discretionary capital projects totalling £120,000 have been halted with no completion dates set. Neither the £60,000 windows replacement nor the £60,000 solar panel installation has any planned spend for 2026/27.
findings.matters: Council deferring discretionary capital investment due to structural uncertainty about its future form, suggesting constrained financial planning during reorganisation period.
findings.figures: Windows replacement budget £60,000, Solar installation budget £60,000, combined forecast £0, combined variance (£120,000)
findings.quote: Works have been deferred due to the uncertainty created by the Local Government Reorganisation.

findings.headline: Epsom Playhouse boiler and air conditioning tenders exceed £510,000 budget; additional authorization required from council and shadow authority.
findings.detail: Replacement costs came in above the approved budget. Both EEBC and the shadow authority must authorize additional spend before works can proceed in August 2027. Only £30,000 is currently forecast to spend from the £510,000 budget.
findings.matters: Cost overrun requires multi-authority sign-off during Local Government Reorganisation, indicating capital planning challenges and execution risk.
findings.figures: Budget £510,000, Year end forecast £30,000, Variance (£480,000)
findings.quote: After receiving tenders, the cost exceeds the budget allocation, authorisation for additional spend is required from EEBC and the shadow authority. Works are planned for August 2027 assuming additional funding agreed.

findings.headline: Uppermill Pond bank replacement cost exceeds budget after tree officer blocks removal requests; project delayed to 2027/28.
findings.detail: The tree officer refused to allow removal of trees near the bank, changing project scope and increasing costs to £299,127, exceeding the £289,230 budget. Value engineering is being explored but only £25,000 of the budget is now forecast to spend this year. The project will not start this financial year.
findings.matters: Cost overruns on infrastructure projects signal planning weaknesses and execution risk; scope changes mid-project indicate potential for further budget creep and delay.
findings.figures: Budget £289,230, Revised estimate £299,127, Year end forecast £25,000, Variance (£264,230)
findings.quote: The revised cost estimate given £299,127 (which does not include the Tree works) exceeds the  budget therefore value engineering measures are being looked at. Realistically this project will not be started this financial year until all issues/risks are investigated.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creates significant uncertainty over capital programme viability, scope and timing.
findings.detail: Paper warns LGR introduces 'significant degree of uncertainty and transition risk' to capital programme management. Changes to funding arrangements, asset ownership, delivery responsibilities and strategic priorities could 'directly affect the viability, scope, and timing of capital schemes currently in development or delivery'.
findings.matters: LGR is material threat to asset maintenance plans and capital strategy continuity; raises fundamental questions about which schemes will proceed and under what governance.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: LGR introduces a significant degree of uncertainty and transition risk that must be carefully considered in the management of the Council's capital programme.

findings.headline: Inflation and rising contractor quotes placing major impact on council's ability to deliver capital projects within budget.
findings.detail: Report explicitly flags that global events and inflation have caused firms to 'significantly increase their quotes for works' and this is having 'a major impact on the Council's ability to source contractors within budget'. Risk is identified as likely to affect both current and future capital projects.
findings.matters: Cost inflation threatens ability to deliver approved capital programme and budget control; may force difficult choices between scope reduction or additional funding.
findings.figures: None specific quantified
findings.quote: Global events and rising inflation have caused firms to significantly increase their quotes for works, having a major impact on the Council's ability to source contractors within budget. This is likely to impact on both current and future capital projects.

findings.headline: £3.057m capital receipt from East Street sale received but against backdrop of capital receipts declining over ten years.
findings.detail: Council received £3.1m sale proceeds (£3.057m net of costs). Paper describes this as bolstering capital receipts reserve and delaying need to borrow for asset maintenance. However, it explicitly notes the reserve 'has diminished over the past 10 years', signalling structural decline in property-generated funding.
findings.matters: While receipt is positive, the long-term declining receipts trend suggests growing structural reliance on borrowing to fund asset maintenance.
findings.figures: £3.057m net receipt, £3.1m gross proceeds, reserves diminished over 10 years
findings.quote: This receipt will bolster the Council's capital receipts reserve which is required to fund capital investment. This reserve has diminished over the past 10 years, and this addition will delay the need to borrow to maintain Council assets.

findings.headline: Council withdraws £49.6m approval to borrow for commercial property due to Local Government Reorganisation uncertainty.
findings.detail: Borrowing authority for commercial property acquisitions is cancelled with no further purchases planned. This was part of the Capital Strategy approved by Full Council in February 2026 but has now been halted due to LGR uncertainty, representing a significant reversal of capital investment strategy.
findings.matters: Major strategic pivot affecting council's commercial property portfolio plans, revenue income assumptions, and available borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: £49.6 million
findings.quote: The approval to borrow up to £49.6 million for the acquisition of commercial property has been withdrawn given Local Government Reorganisation, and no further purchases will take place.

findings.headline: Capital programme shows £2.488m forecast underspend as major schemes roll forward into next year.
findings.detail: Forecast outturn £3.547m against £6.035m approved budget. Major schemes delayed include Bourne Hall Replacement Heating & Ventilation (£940k), Epsom Playhouse Boiler and air conditioning (£480k), and Bourne Hall Lodge refurbishment (£320k). Section 151 Officer states majority reflects reprofiling rather than cancellation of projects.
findings.matters: Delays to asset maintenance programmes threaten service continuity and may increase future costs if works become more expensive.
findings.figures: £2.488m variance, £3.547m forecast outturn vs £6.035m approved, £940,000 Bourne Hall heating, £480,000 Playhouse boiler, £320,000 Lodge refurbishment
findings.quote: The variance of £2.488 million has arisen due to schemes rolling into the next financial year, or as a result of the works coming in under budget.

findings.headline: Government announcement of 28 October 2025 to reorganize Surrey councils into unitary authorities is freezing the council's capital investment and creating medium-term strategic uncertainty
findings.detail: On 28 October 2025, the Government announced that current county, district and borough councils in Surrey will be replaced by two new unitary authorities. This announcement is directly causing the council to halt its capital investment programme (as evidenced by the £49.6m property acquisition forecast not being executed). The timing and detailed arrangements of the transition remain unclear.
findings.matters: Local government reorganization creates institutional uncertainty and disrupts medium-term planning; lenders would want to understand transition arrangements, the status of existing borrowing commitments, and whether the council can meet its obligations during the restructuring.
findings.figures: Announcement date: 28 October 2025
findings.quote: On 28 October 2025, the Government announced that the current county, district, and borough councils in Surrey will be replaced by two new unitary authorities.

findings.headline: 2024/25 financing cost ratio restated upward by 3 percentage points due to omission of lease assets in IFRS16 implementation
findings.detail: Council identified that private sector landlord lease assets used for temporary accommodation were accidentally omitted from the 2024/25 calculation when implementing IFRS16 on the balance sheet, understating the prior year ratio from 2% to -1%. The error was only discovered during 2025/26 closedown, requiring a material prior year restatement.
findings.matters: A material prior year restatement raises questions about the completeness of the control environment and financial statement accuracy during accounting standard transitions; lenders would want assurance over the integrity of reported figures.
findings.figures: 2024/25 ratio restated from -1% to 2% (3 percentage point correction)
findings.quote: Private Sector Landlord leased properties used for temporary accommodation were accidentally missed from the figures used to deprive the 2024/25 actual of -1%, but when included they bring the figure up to the correct position which is 2%.

findings.headline: Capital forecasts significantly understated: actual spending 5% of estimate, external debt 57% of estimate, CFR 60% of estimate
findings.detail: Council forecast capital expenditure of £58.3m but spent £2.8m; estimated external debt of £115.9m but actual £65.5m; estimated CFR of £139.6m but actual £83.5m; estimated net borrowing of £91.5m but actual £46.2m. The variance is entirely driven by non-execution of the £49.6m commercial property programme. The Chief Finance Officer confirms the council remained in compliance with prudential borrowing controls.
findings.matters: Material variances between prudential forecast and actual indicate either poor forecasting or significant unforecasted changed circumstances; either raises questions about forecasting reliability and financial planning that would concern a lender.
findings.figures: Capital expenditure £2,758k vs £58,258k (4.7%); external debt £65,525k vs £115,873k (56.6%); CFR £83,539k vs £139,570k (59.8%)
findings.quote: The Chief Finance Officer reports that the Council complied with the requirement to keep net borrowing below the CFR in 2025/26, and no difficulties are envisaged for the current or future years.

findings.headline: Financing cost ratio more than tripled to 7% from 2% as cash interest income fell and lease costs rose
findings.detail: The ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream increased from 2% in 2024/25 to 7% in 2025/26 (actual vs estimated 19%), driven by reduced interest on cash balances and increased costs from leased assets under IFRS16. Investments fell from £21.9m to £19.3m. The council states these costs are fully funded by property investment company returns.
findings.matters: Rising financing costs as a proportion of revenue is a material pressure on general fund finances; a lender would want to monitor this trend and understand whether the council can sustain it as cash balances decline.
findings.figures: Financing ratio 2% (2024/25) to 7% (2025/26 actual) vs 19% estimated; investments £21,866k to £19,300k
findings.quote: 2025/26's ratio is higher than 2024/25 principally because of reduced interest on cash balances compared to 2024/25 and also increased leased asset costs. In practice, the financing costs are fully funded by further income generated from both the Council's and Epsom & Ewell Property Investment Company's investment property acquisitions.

findings.headline: Council ceases all further commercial property acquisitions following October 2025 government announcement of unitary authority reorganization
findings.detail: Council estimated £58.3m capital expenditure for 2025/26 including £49.6m for commercial properties, but spent £2.8m with zero on property acquisition. Following the Government's 28 October 2025 announcement that current county, district and borough councils in Surrey will be replaced by two new unitary authorities, the council has halted the Commercial Property Acquisition Fund programme that has operated since 2016/17 with planned borrowing of up to £380m.
findings.matters: The commercial property investment programme was central to the council's financial model and capital spending plans; halting it marks a major strategic reversal that fundamentally changes the council's future borrowing and investment trajectory.
findings.figures: Capital expenditure estimated £58,258k vs actual £2,758k; commercial properties estimated £49,569k vs actual £0k
findings.quote: Consequently, the Council does not anticipate making any further property purchases under the Commercial Property Acquisition Fund programme.

findings.headline: External debt remained stable at £64.4m with no requirement for temporary borrowing.
findings.detail: The council's Public Works Loans Board debt stayed flat at £64.4m throughout the year (unchanged from March 2025). Despite declining average cash balances, no temporary borrowing was required during 2025/26, indicating the council managed its working capital within existing resources.
findings.matters: A stable debt position with no emergency borrowing needs provides reassurance to lenders about the council's ability to manage its cash position, though the trajectory of declining cash reserves warrants monitoring.
findings.figures: PWLB external debt £64.4m (unchanged from March 2025)
findings.quote: No temporary borrowings were required in 2025/26.

findings.headline: Treasury performance beat forecast and benchmark by substantial margins despite headwinds.
findings.detail: The council achieved net investment income of £1,178,313, exceeding its mid-year forecast of £1,042,000 by £236,313 (22.7%). The average gross return of 4.38% outperformed the SONIA benchmark of 4.01% by 37 basis points, delivering net returns of 4.23%. This outperformance occurred despite lower cash balances and declining interest rates.
findings.matters: Despite unfavorable market conditions and a shrinking cash base, the council's treasury management delivered superior returns, demonstrating competent portfolio management and effective optimization of available resources.
findings.figures: Net income £1,178,313 vs forecast £1,042,000 (outperformance £236,313 or 22.7%); average return 4.38% vs SONIA 4.01% (outperformance 37bp); net return 4.23%
findings.quote: The net outturn position exceeded the mid-year forecast reported to the Financial Strategy Advisory Group in November 2025, when it was anticipated that net income from investments would be £1,042,000 at the end of the year.

findings.headline: Investment income fell to £1.22m from £1.56m as cash balances and interest rates declined.
findings.detail: Gross interest earned fell by £336,587 (21.6%) from £1,556,683 to £1,220,096. The reduction is attributed to both lower average cash balances (down £2.3m) and lower average returns during the year. Since investment income contributes to funding council services, this represents a material reduction in the council's own-source revenue.
findings.matters: Investment returns help balance the council's budget; declining returns reduce financial flexibility and increase reliance on other funding sources, particularly concerning in a period of strained local government finances.
findings.quote: During 2025/26, the Council earned £1,220,096 in gross interest from its treasury investments, compared to £1,556,683 in 2024/25. The reduction reflects both lower average cash balances, which fell by £2.3m to £27.8m, and lower average gross returns during the year (see section 3.4).

findings.headline: Average cash reserves fell by 7.6% year-on-year to £27.8m despite stable debt position.
findings.detail: The council's average cash balance declined by £2.3m compared to the prior year, falling to £27.8m. Year-end treasury investments also fell from £19.8m to £19.3m. Despite this tighter cash position, no temporary borrowing was required, suggesting tight but adequate liquidity management through the year.
findings.matters: A declining cash position indicates the council's liquidity buffer is shrinking; a lender needs to understand whether this represents a structural trend or temporary variation, as continuing declines would threaten financial resilience.
findings.figures: Cash balance fell £2.3m to £27.8m; year-end investments £19.3m (down from £19.8m); external PWLB debt £64.4m (unchanged)
findings.quote: lower average cash balances, which fell by £2.3m to £27.8m

findings.headline: Balanced 2026/27 budget significantly supported by non-recurring or volatile government grant uplifts that do not extend into years 2 and 3
findings.detail: The £3.083m favourable movement that eliminated the original £1.928m deficit includes £1.410m from FFR uplift (based on recognition of temporary accommodation costs in funding formula) and £743k from EPR grant outperformance (council received £1.080m against MTFS assumption of £0.337m). Neither of these movements are reflected in Years 2–3 forecasts, and the MTFS still shows gaps of £206k (Year 2) and £373k (Year 3).
findings.matters: The balanced budget is materially dependent on grant income that the council has not assumed will continue; Years 2–3 structural gaps suggest the council faces renewed pressure once these improve once-off benefits unwind.
findings.figures: FFR uplift Year 1 £1.410m (£0m Years 2–3); EPR grant uplift £0.743m Year 1 only; three-year gap reduced from £5.063m to £0.579m (Years 2–3 still £579k cumulatively)
findings.quote: During the summer of 2025, changes to the provisional government funding formula, particularly the recognition of actual expenditure on temporary accommodation, indicated that the Council might benefit rather than lose funding...the Council ultimately received £1.080m, a positive movement of £0.743m.

findings.headline: Budget balance dependent on £1.35m annual dividend from two commercial properties held by wholly-owned subsidiary outside the borough
findings.detail: The council explicitly relies on dividend from EEPIC (Epsom & Ewell Property Investment Company) to balance the budget. The two commercial properties are held outside the borough and were acquired in 2017 before new statutory guidance restricted such acquisitions. The council holds £5.7m Property Income Equalisation Reserve specifically to mitigate loss of this income.
findings.matters: Property income is volatile and concentrated in a single subsidiary; tenant default, property value decline, or market conditions could force immediate reserve drawdown at a council already running at minimum buffers.
findings.figures: £1.35m dividend expected 2026/27; £5.7m Property Income Equalisation Reserve held against loss of income
findings.quote: The Council's 2025/26 budget includes £1.35m expected dividend income from Epsom and Ewell Property Investment Company, generated from its two commercial properties. This is on track to be fully received this financial year and will continue into 2026/27. The council relies on dividend from its commercial properties to balance the budget. In the event of loss of dividend, the council holds prudent level of Property Income Equalisation Reserve, £5.7m, to counter the loss.

findings.headline: General Fund reserve at minimum with only £55k buffer; Corporate Projects reserve being drawn to cover current-year deficit
findings.detail: The General Fund working balance is £1.555m against a £1.5m minimum, leaving only £55k flexibility. The 2025/26 projected £520k deficit is being funded from the Corporate Projects reserve, depleting it from £2.495m to £1.975m. Uncommitted reserves available for general use drop from £6.593m to £3.530m after commitments.
findings.matters: A council running reserves at minimum with no buffer cannot absorb unexpected costs or income shortfalls; further draws on restricted reserves signal financial stress.
findings.figures: General Fund £1.555m vs £1.5m minimum (£55k buffer); Corporate Projects reserve reduced by £520k from £2.495m to £1.975m; total uncommitted reserves (General Fund + Corporate Projects) £3.530m
findings.quote: The General Fund reserve currently stands at £1.555m, only £55,000 above the £1.5m minimum balance approved by Council in July 2025. Therefore, it is suggested that this deficit is met from the Corporate Projects reserve, decreasing the uncommitted balance from £2,495,000 to £1,975,000.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation demand and costs creating ongoing pressure despite budget increase
findings.detail: The council projected a £520k deficit in 2025/26 mainly from higher demand for housing and homelessness services. To address this, it has increased nightly paid accommodation budget by £750k over the MTFS period (£250k annually), yet forecast pressures of £250k per year continue into Years 2 and 3, suggesting costs are outpacing the increase.
findings.matters: Rising demand for high-cost services creates structural budget pressures that may exceed reserves if growth continues beyond forecast or if government resets FFR benefits.
findings.figures: £520k projected 2025/26 deficit; £750k budget increase over MTFS; £250k annual pressure Years 2–3; net budget increase in Community & Wellbeing from £5.798m to £7.161m (1.363m increase)
findings.quote: The projected deficit is mainly due to the higher demand for housing/homelessness services...Community & Wellbeing Committee agreed to recommend service estimates for 2026/27 to Full Council...which include a net increase of budget for nightly paid accommodation costs of £750,000 to address the rising cost in this area.

findings.headline: Health & Safety Executive investigation into December 2021 waste collection vehicle incident could result in settlement payment with provision set aside
findings.detail: The council has made a provision for the outcome of an HSE investigation into a December 2021 incident involving a waste collection vehicle. This outstanding matter could result in a settlement payment that would impact the waste collection budget (c.£1.4m income).
findings.matters: An unresolved regulatory matter with financial exposure that could materialise during the 2026/27 budget year.
findings.figures: c.£1.4m waste collection income at risk; provision set aside (amount not disclosed)
findings.quote: The Health & Safety Executive (HSE) investigation into December 2021's incident involving a waste collection vehicle could result in a settlement payment. Provision set-aside for outcome of HSE investigation.

findings.headline: Pension fund deficit of £6m (IAS19 basis) will be addressed through triennial review outcome, impact factored into 2026/27 budget once completed
findings.detail: The council has a £6m pension fund deficit on an IAS19 accounting basis. The triennial actuarial review outcome is pending, and its impact on pension contribution rates will be factored into the 2026/27 budget once completed. This represents a known but not-yet-quantified cost pressure.
findings.matters: A material unfunded liability where the actual cost impact for 2026/27 is still unknown but will reduce available revenue once the actuarial review is finalised.
findings.figures: £6m deficit on IAS19 basis as at 31 March 2025
findings.quote: Impact of triennial review of pension contributions to be factored into 2026/27 budget, once completed

findings.headline: Council property investment company (EEPIC Properties) rated high risk for loss of rental income or tenant failure (£1.3m impact)
findings.detail: The council's property investment company is exposed to significant revenue risk through loss of rental income, tenant failure, or prolonged void periods. This would directly reduce the council's revenue position and create budgetary pressures. The mitigation relies on regular reporting and maintaining prudent reserves.
findings.matters: A high-rated risk where the council's own investment asset could directly reduce available revenue, competing with service reserves for mitigation.
findings.figures: £1.3m high impact rating
findings.quote: This increases the likelihood of loss of rental income, tenant failure, or prolonged void periods, which would directly reduce the Council's revenue position and create budgetary pressures.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation funding from government described as 'woefully inadequate', creating pressure on reserves
findings.detail: The government has provided only £0.380m across all Surrey councils for LGR transition costs, which the council describes as 'woefully inadequate' and creates pressure on reserves and threatens day-to-day service budgets. The council is attempting mitigation by strengthening financial reserves, with £454k currently allocated in strategic priorities reserves for LGR.
findings.matters: A significant external cost driver (£1m impact rated high) where government funding is acknowledged as insufficient, forcing councils to draw on reserves for essential transition activity.
findings.figures: £1.00m high-impact LGR risk; £0.380m provided across all Surrey councils; £454k allocated in strategic priorities reserves for LGR
findings.quote: £0.380m provided across all Surrey councils is "woefully inadequate", creating pressure on reserves and threatening day-to-day service budgets

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs forecast to overspend by over £1m in 2025/26, with 2026/27 budget increased significantly
findings.detail: The council is explicitly driving the failure-to-balance-budget risk through rising temporary accommodation costs. A forecast overspend of over £1m is already materialising in 2025/26, and the 2026/27 budget has been increased significantly to address this adverse position. The underlying issue is a significant increase in households requiring temporary accommodation and lack of affordable housing preventing move-out.
findings.matters: A demand-driven cost that has already overrun in the current year signals ongoing pressure on the revenue budget and limited council control over the driver.
findings.figures: over £1m forecast overspend 2025/26; £4.4m net expenditure homelessness budget 2026/27
findings.quote: Given TA is driving a forecast overspend of over £1m for 2025/26, implement targeted actions to reduce demand and cost

findings.headline: S106 and CIL reserves projected to be fully consumed by 2028/29
findings.detail: Developer contribution reserves (S106: £1.7m currently, forecast £0 by 2028/29; CIL: £9.8m currently, forecast £6.9m by 2028/29) are being deployed to fund capital works. These are project-specific and once spent cannot be replaced from revenue.
findings.matters: Once these restricted reserves are spent, all capital funding must come from council's own revenue and borrowing. This reduces future capital flexibility unless new developer contributions arrive.
findings.figures: S106 reserves: 2024/25 actual £1,703k, declining to £0 by 2028/29. CIL reserves: 2024/25 actual £9,804k, declining to £6,983k
findings.quote: S106 funds: 2024/25 Actual 1,703 / 2026/27 Estimate 402 / 2028/29 Estimate 0. CIL: 2024/25 Actual 9,804 / 2026/27 Estimate 7,983 / 2028/29 Estimate 6,983

findings.headline: Council maintaining under-borrowed position (£17m under-borrowing by 2026/27) while cash reserves decline
findings.detail: The council is deliberately borrowing less than its Capital Financing Requirement allows, using cash reserves instead. By 2026/27, the CFR is £81.5m but gross debt is only £64.5m, leaving £17m under-borrowed. This strategy assumes rates will fall, but is vulnerable if rates rise or cash needs increase.
findings.matters: A lender should understand that the council has chosen not to lock in current borrowing costs. If cash balances decline further and the council must borrow later at higher rates, this becomes a risk to affordability.
findings.figures: Capital Financing Requirement 2026/27: £81,524k. Actual gross debt 2026/27 estimate: £64,508k. Under-borrowing: £17,016k
findings.quote: The Council is currently maintaining an under-borrowed position. This means that the capital borrowing need (the Capital Financing Requirement) has not been fully funded with loan debt and the Council's cash balances have been used instead as a temporary measure.

findings.headline: Earmarked reserves depleting by 59% as council winds down ahead of unitary merger
findings.detail: Earmarked revenue reserves declining from £19.7m to £8.1m over the forecast period. This shows deliberate reserve drawdown to fund capital or close budget gaps, consistent with an orderly transition but indicating fewer retained contingencies.
findings.matters: Earmarked reserves represent the council's policy commitments and contingency capacity. A 59% decline signals the council is consuming previously-set-aside funding, reducing future flexibility.
findings.figures: Earmarked revenue reserves: 2024/25 actual £19,736k; 2026/27 estimate £12,631k; 2028/29 estimate £8,084k
findings.quote: Earmarked revenue reserves: 2024/25 Actual 19,736 / 2026/27 Estimate 12,631 / 2028/29 Estimate 8,084

findings.headline: Authorised borrowing limit cut by £55m reflecting organisational dissolution
findings.detail: The maximum permitted debt level is being reduced from £145m to £90m for 2026/27 and beyond. This £55m reduction in headroom reflects the council's transition to the new unitary authority and its reduced capital programme.
findings.matters: A lender assessing the council needs to know that borrowing capacity is being deliberately constrained ahead of the reorganisation. This signals wind-down rather than expansion and reduces the council's flexibility if unexpected costs emerge.
findings.figures: Authorised Limit 2024/25: £145m debt + £3m OLTL = £148m total. Authorised Limit 2026/27: £90m debt + £3m OLTL = £93m total
findings.quote: Debt relating to commercial property fund... Total [Authorised Limit]: 2024/25 Estimate 148,000 / 2026/27 Estimate 93,000

findings.headline: Commercial property borrowing programme abandoned due to local government reorganisation
findings.detail: The council had approved an £80m Commercial Property Acquisition Fund in 2017 for prudential borrowing. This has been halted entirely because the council is being replaced by a new unitary authority, East Surrey, from October 2025 onwards. No further property purchases are planned under this scheme.
findings.matters: The loss of an income-yielding asset acquisition programme affects medium-term revenue sustainability and signals that capital strategy is now in wind-down mode rather than growth mode.
findings.figures: £80m approved limit on Commercial Property Acquisition Fund; £0 forecast spend 2026/27 onwards
findings.quote: Council agreed in February 2017 to extend the limit of the Commercial Property Acquisition Fund to £80m, to be financed from Prudential Borrowing. On 28 October 2025, the Government announced that the current county, district, and borough councils in Surrey will be replaced by two new unitary authorities. Consequently, the Council does not anticipate making any further property purchases under the Commercial Property Acquisition Fund programme.

findings.headline: Capital programme cost forecasts are six years old and acknowledged as materially understated by inflation
findings.detail: The 2027/28–2030/31 capital programme is based on the Asset Management Plan approved in July 2020 (six years prior to this February 2026 strategy). The Council explicitly states that costs have increased since 2020 and will be updated 'when budgets for those relevant financial years come to be set'. No current inflation adjustment is provided.
findings.matters: Capital programme forecasts may significantly understate actual costs. As budgets are set, schemes may be deferred, scaled back, or require additional funding, affecting the Council's ability to maintain assets and service infrastructure.
findings.figures: Asset Management Plan approval: July 2020; Strategy period: 2027/28–2030/31
findings.quote: Forecasts for 2027/28 to 2030/31 are based on the estimated cost of works as reported in the Asset Management Plan 2020-2030. It is acknowledged that due to inflation, costs will have increased since this Asset Management Plan was agreed at S&R in July 2020.

findings.headline: Revenue contributions to capital programme eliminated from 2026/27, reducing financing flexibility
findings.detail: The Council has removed revenue funding from its capital financing model from 2026/27 onwards. Previously, revenue reserves (such as repairs and renewals reserve) contributed to capital funding; the 2025/26 forecast showed £0.50m of revenue contributions, but from 2026/27 onwards this is assumed to be £0m.
findings.matters: Removal of revenue funding constrains the Council's ability to respond to capital investment needs and increases reliance on capital receipts, external grants, and developer contributions—sources which are limited or time-bound.
findings.figures: Revenue funding 2025/26: £0.50m; 2026/27 onwards: £0.00m
findings.quote: From 2026/27, it is assumed the capital programme will no longer be funded by any revenue contributions.

findings.headline: Major capital project (Town Hall relocation) cancelled in 2025/26 due to Local Government Reorganisation uncertainty
findings.detail: The Council had planned to relocate its civic offices to a new Town Hall site. This project was cancelled in 2025/26 due to uncertainty from the Local Government Reorganisation process, representing a significant revision to the Council's capital strategy.
findings.matters: Cancelled major projects signal strategic uncertainty and may have incurred sunk costs. It indicates the Council's ability to plan and execute long-term capital investment is constrained by external policy changes.
findings.figures: Cancellation date: 2025/26
findings.quote: The Council had planned to move its civic offices to a new Town Hall site. This project was cancelled in 2025/26 due to the uncertainty due to the Local Government Reorganisation.

findings.headline: Capital Receipts Reserve forecast negative from 2026/27: £1.98m (31 March 2026), declining to -£0.88m (31 March 2027) and -£2.34m (31 March 2030); target minimum £1m
findings.detail: The Council's capital receipts reserve is projected to become negative from 2026/27 onwards, declining from £1.98m (31 March 2026) to -£0.88m by 31 March 2027, reaching -£2.34m by 2029/30. This occurs because annual capital programme spending exceeds available capital receipts each year. The Council's Medium Term Financial Strategy targets a minimum capital reserve of £1m as contingency.
findings.matters: A council forecasting negative capital reserves cannot sustain its capital programme without either asset sales, external funding, revenue contributions (now stopped), or borrowing. This represents a material constraint on financial flexibility and investment capacity.
findings.figures: Capital Receipts at 31/3/2026: £1.98m; projected at 31/3/2027: -£0.88m; at 31/3/2029: -£1.71m; at 31/3/2030: -£2.34m. Target minimum: £1m
findings.quote: The forecast of capital receipts at 31 March 2026 is £1.97million... Estimated resources at 31/3/2027: Capital Receipts (0.88)

findings.headline: IFRS 16 lease accounting now on balance sheet: £0.65m right-of-use assets and £1.76m lease liabilities recognised in first implementation year
findings.detail: First year of mandatory IFRS 16 implementation. The council has recognised lease liabilities of £1.76m and right-of-use assets of £0.65m on the balance sheet. Previously these would have been off-balance-sheet. Audit testing on lease samples and documentation was still outstanding at time of report drafting.
findings.matters: IFRS 16 brings lease commitments onto the balance sheet, materially changing reported leverage and asset coverage. A lender needs to understand the scale and nature of these newly-disclosed commitments, which moved from contingent to actual liabilities.
findings.figures: Lease liabilities £1.76m; ROU assets £0.65m
findings.quote: The Council's 2024/25 draft accounts disclose a right of use asset balance of £0.65m and Lease liabilities of £1.76m.

findings.headline: Council declined to implement prior-year audit recommendations for property valuations and related-party controls, citing budget constraints
findings.detail: Management continues not to conduct annual valuations of all investment properties despite a prior-year audit recommendation. It rejected both this recommendation and a separate related-party control recommendation, arguing that resources are under significant pressure and the recommendations are disproportionate to the identified risks.
findings.matters: Persistent rejection of audit recommendations, even when formally documented as issues, suggests either audit advice is not commanding action or financial constraints are preventing control improvements. Both are governance concerns for a lender.
findings.figures: Seven investment properties worth £50k (below materiality threshold) not formally revalued annually
findings.quote: The Council does not consider the additional resources required to adopt the recommendation to be either essential or proportionate, particularly as Council budgets and resources are under significant pressure.

findings.headline: Pension liability contains £531k undervaluation from fund auditors; council left adjustment unposted as immaterial
findings.detail: Surrey Pension Fund auditors identified a £26.542m undervaluation of level 3 investments across the fund; the council's allocated share is approximately £531k. The council's own IAS 19 pension net liability stands at £6.7m (after asset ceiling adjustment), a significant swing from a £2.3m net asset in the prior year. Management did not adjust the accounts for the £531k difference, treating it as immaterial.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities are a major element of council balance sheets and fund valuations are sensitive to investment market assumptions. A £531k uncorrected difference in a £6.7m liability creates measurement uncertainty that a lender should be aware of.
findings.figures: Fund undervaluation £26.542m; council share £531k; pension net liability £6.7m (moved from £2.3m asset)
findings.quote: The Surrey Pension Fund auditors identified a £26.542m undervaluation of level 3 investments. The Council's share of this difference is approximately £531k. Management did not adjust the accounts as the amount is immaterial.

findings.headline: Key personnel departure created data control gap; internal surveyor left without retaining documentation of valuation inputs to external expert
findings.detail: Auditor identified the root cause of valuation discrepancies: the previous internal surveyor departed after providing data to valuers but did not retain copies of what was provided. This prevented reconciliation and caused audit delays. The new surveyor, with property and finance support, has now resolved outstanding items, but the control gap created timeline pressure on audit completion.
findings.matters: Loss of documented handover and retained records when key personnel leave is a control weakness. It delayed a statutory audit and required reconstructive work. It signals institutional knowledge concentration and potential future continuity risk.
findings.figures: Audit delayed beyond end-December 2025 target; backstop date 27 February 2026
findings.quote: The issue occurred due to the departure of the previous internal surveyor, who provided the required information to the valuer but did not retain a copy of it. This led to delay in the completion of the work on Other land and buildings valuation and Investment properties valuation.

findings.headline: Investment property valuations contain £149k error; auditor identified discrepancies in rental amounts and lease terms versus council records
findings.detail: Testing of investment property samples identified discrepancies between data provided to the council's valuation expert (Wilks Head and Eve) and supporting records held by the council. The auditor quantified the net impact as £149k overstatement. Management declined to adjust, treating it as immaterial. This remains an unadjusted misstatement.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence in asset valuations. Investment properties total £63.6m (council) / £112.9m (group). Documented discrepancies between expert valuations and underlying records suggest data quality or control issues that could affect reliability of the balance sheet.
findings.figures: £149k net valuation difference; investment properties £63.6m (council)
findings.quote: Testing on Investment property sample identified discrepancies in the current rental amount and lease term used by your expert when compared to the supporting records held by Council. This resulted in net impact difference of £149k in valuation.

findings.headline: Scenario planning has not been implemented despite repeated audit recommendation, leaving financial risk assumptions unchallenged and budget pressure blind spots.
findings.detail: The 2024/25 budget assumed 70 households in nightly paid accommodation but actual was 90 at year-end, and 116 in Q1 2025/26. The audit notes the Council had not done scenario or sensitivity analysis to stress-test this assumption, and external consultants were engaged in 2025 to do modelling work. This signals internal planning capability gaps.
findings.matters: Scenario planning is how councils anticipate and absorb shocks. Its absence means budget pressures arrive as crises rather than anticipated risks, forcing reactive reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: Budget assumption 70 households vs actual 116 in Q1 2025/26 (66% variance not anticipated)
findings.quote: The Council would benefit from scenario planning, to provide greater transparency around financial risk, for key financial assumptions as that would have identified the worst and realistic case scenarios around the demand led homelessness service

findings.headline: Fraud governance limited to annual reporting to members, restricting visibility and agility in detecting and responding to in-year fraud risk.
findings.detail: Fraud reporting occurs only once per year (November), despite the audit recommending more frequent reporting (twice annually or quarterly). The Council shares counter-fraud work plans but once a year. This is particularly concerning given homelessness spending pressures and demand-led service pressures.
findings.matters: Annual fraud reporting creates a 12-month gap in member visibility over fraud activity and investigations. With high-risk services (homelessness, property investment) under pressure, more frequent oversight is prudent.
findings.figures: Annual fraud reporting only; last report November 2024, next planned November 2025
findings.quote: Fraud reporting to Members currently occurs annually, which limits visibility of in-year activity

findings.headline: Capital programme slipped £2.249m (30% of budget), signalling delivery challenges or reprioritisation amid Local Government Reorganisation uncertainty.
findings.detail: Actual capital expenditure was £5.116m against a £7.365m budget, a 30% slip. The £7m Town Hall relocation project was cancelled in May 2025 due to LGR uncertainty. This reduces near-term capital pressure but signals the council is operating in transition mode and may struggle to execute planned capital delivery.
findings.matters: Capital slippage can indicate either prudent cash management or delivery failure. Combined with LGR transition and governance distraction, it suggests the council may not deliver planned service infrastructure improvements.
findings.figures: £5.116m actual vs £7.365m budget, £2.249m slippage (30%), £7m Town Hall project cancelled
findings.quote: actual expenditure was £5.116 million, some £2.249 million less than the £7.365 million budget due to slippage

findings.headline: Internal audit issued one 'No Assurance' rating (Environmental Health Food Safety) and three 'Limited Assurance' ratings, marking a deterioration from prior year.
findings.detail: Of 18 planned audits, 88% were completed by year-end (June 2025), below the 95% target due to capacity constraints. Limited Assurance was given to Affordable Housing, Information Governance, and Main Accounting. No Assurance to Environmental Health Food Safety is new; prior year had no No Assurance ratings. Recommendation completion is lagging with revised deadlines required.
findings.matters: Food safety and main accounting assurance gaps are operational and financial control red flags. Capacity constraints in internal audit itself signal broader governance strain, and lenders need to know core financial systems are under question.
findings.figures: 1 No Assurance, 3 Limited Assurance ratings, 88% audit completion (below 95% target), 35 recommendations issued with 80% completed by July 2025
findings.quote: Three areas received Limited Assurance—Affordable Housing, Information Governance, and Main Accounting—and one No Assurance—Environmental Health Food Safety. This marks a slight deterioration from the prior year, which had no 'No Assurance ratings'

findings.headline: Subsidiary company income fell 45% short of budget, requiring £700k reserve drawdown to offset underperformance.
findings.detail: Epsom & Ewell Property Investment Company (EEPIC) returned £769k against a £1.4m budget (55% shortfall) due to a lease amendment at one property. The shortfall was covered by drawing £700k from the Property Income Equalisation Reserve. For 2025/26, EEPIC income is forecast to recover to £1.35m with no planned reserve withdrawal.
findings.matters: The council depends on property investment returns to close its budget gap, but income is volatile and the reserve backing that income is being depleted. A second income shock would force deeper cuts.
findings.figures: £769k actual vs £1.4m budget (£631k shortfall, 45%), £700k reserve drawdown, £1.35m forecast 2025/26
findings.quote: dividend and recharge income from EEPIC was £769k, significantly below the £1.4m budget due to a lease amendment at one property. This shortfall was mitigated by a £700k draw from the Property Income Equalisation Reserve

findings.headline: General Fund Reserve of only £1.5m (around 17% of net revenue expenditure) being drawn down to fund revenue pressures, with no clear replenishment plan.
findings.detail: The 2024/25 budget saw a 2.7% overspend of £242k funded from reserves. Q1 2025/26 required partial use of the £400k contingency, with the remaining gap expected to draw further from reserves. The audit notes the Council has not yet reflected the full 2025/26 forecast impact in its MTFP.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion is accelerating and the MTFP lags actual pressures. If reserves fall below £1m, the council loses its buffer for shocks and becomes reliant on exceptional support.
findings.figures: General Fund Reserve £1.5m, 2024/25 overspend £242k, Q1 2025/26 overspend £875k, £400k contingency partially used, earmarked reserves £13.63m
findings.quote: The 2025/26 forecast is a £475k overspend partially funded by £400k contingency, but the remaining gap needs to be funded from reserves which has yet to be reflected in the Council's MTFP

findings.headline: Medium-term funding gap of at least £4.095 million by 2027/28, with savings delivery plans consistently unmet and undershooting targets.
findings.detail: The July 2025 MTFP showed a cumulative gap of £5.06m by 2028/29. Savings of £326k were achieved in 2024/25 (92% of £354k target), but the planned 2026/27 savings were cut from £450k to £150k after homelessness savings were deemed unachievable. The Council has delivered £700k in savings identification for 2025/26, but closing a multi-year gap requires sustained delivery.
findings.matters: The council is relying on reserves to fund day-to-day operations and has not yet articulated a credible path to balance. External consultants were hired (Pixel, LG Futures) to strengthen modelling, suggesting internal capacity constraints.
findings.figures: £5.06m cumulative gap to 2028/29 (July 2025), £4.095m gap to 2027/28 (September 2025), £700k savings identified for 2025/26, £123k planned for 2025/26, £150k for 2026/27 (down from £450k)
findings.quote: the gap to 2027/28 has now increased to £4.095 million in September 2025 and the Council needs to safeguard its diminishing reserves

findings.headline: Homelessness structural deficit grew to £875k overspend in Q1 2025/26 with no clear funded solution through the MTFP.
findings.detail: The 2024/25 budget assumed 70 households in nightly paid accommodation but ended with 90. Q1 2025/26 saw 116 households at an average cost, driving an £885k forecast overspend for the year. Despite investment in Housing First and prevention officers, demand continues to outpace the funded budget, requiring drawdown from reserves.
findings.matters: Homelessness is demand-led and uncontrollable, signalling a structural problem the council cannot solve within its current resource envelope. Lenders need to know this is consuming reserves and will persist.
findings.figures: £581k 2024/25 adverse variance, £875k Q1 2025/26 overspend, £885k full-year 2025/26 forecast, budgeted 70 households vs actual 116 in Q1
findings.quote: increased demand for homelessness in 25/26 has resulted in a negative year end forecast of £885k

findings.headline: Commercial property acquisition borrowing facility unlikely to be used due to Local Government Reorganisation
findings.detail: Council holds £49.6m approved borrowing headroom (not a reserve, but a limit for potential investment). Described as 'increasingly unlikely to be progressed in the near term' given LGR context.
findings.matters: Signals that LGR has created sufficient uncertainty to pause strategic capital plans; lenders should understand that council's capital strategy is now on hold pending clarity on reorganisation structure and asset ownership.
findings.figures: £49,600,000 available borrowing headroom
findings.quote: Given the current context of Local Government Reorganisation, it is increasingly unlikely that this facility will be progressed in the near term.

findings.headline: Stew Ponds silt removal project deferred after financial strategy group declined to recommend additional funding
findings.detail: Budgeted project required additional capital funding beyond the £150k budget. Following FSAG's review in September 2025, the additional funding was not recommended to be progressed. FSAG requested Environment committee consider next steps in January 2026.
findings.matters: Shows that environmental maintenance and asset condition projects are being rejected when they exceed initial budget, suggesting deferred maintenance will accumulate unless budget discipline changes.
findings.figures: £150,000 underspend
findings.quote: Stew Ponds removal of silt project which shows an underspend of £150,000, required additional capital funding which was not recommended to be progressed following FSAG's review of initial proposals on 26 September 2025.

findings.headline: Rising inflation significantly impacting council's ability to source contractors within capital budget
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that global events and rising inflation have caused firms to significantly increase their quotes for works, with major impact on ability to source contractors within budget. This is identified as likely to impact both current and future capital projects.
findings.matters: Indicates structural cost pressure that will constrain capital delivery going forward; lenders need to understand whether this will cause deferred maintenance, project deferrals, or require additional financing.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: Global events and rising inflation have caused firms to significantly increase their quotes for works, having a major impact on the Council's ability to source contractors within budget. This is likely to impact on both current and future capital projects.

findings.headline: Two capital schemes paused pending approval of additional funding beyond budget
findings.detail: Ashley Centre car park waterproof membrane (budgeted £184k) and Uppermill Pond bank replacement (budgeted £150k) are paused awaiting additional funding. FSAG supported the request in November 2025 and Environment committee will review in January 2026. For Uppermill Pond, if additional funding is not agreed, £25k currently forecast would need to transfer to revenue.
findings.matters: Signals cost overrun risk on individual capital projects and delivery delays; shows schemes cannot proceed within approved budgets and may consume revenue resources if additional capital funding is not approved.
findings.figures: £184,000 (Ashley Centre), £150,000 (Uppermill Pond), £25,000 forecast Uppermill Pond requiring revenue transfer if additional funding not agreed
findings.quote: Two schemes have been paused due to additional funds being required; the Ashley Centre car park waterproof membrane scheme, budgeted at £184,000; and the Uppermill Pond Bank replacement scheme budgeted at £150,000. There is a current forecast of £25,000 against the Uppermill Pond scheme which will need to be transferred to revenue should the additional funding not be agreed.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation flagged as presenting 'significant uncertainty and transition risk' that must be actively considered in budget planning.
findings.detail: Section 12.6-12.7 explicitly state that LGR 'presents a significant degree of uncertainty and transition risk' affecting financial planning. The authority notes that 'potential changes to funding streams, service delivery responsibilities, and strategic priorities may emerge' that could 'directly influence the assumptions underpinning the revenue budget, requiring ongoing review and adjustment.'
findings.matters: LGR uncertainty makes forward financial assumptions fragile; boundary changes could alter funding allocations, service scope, and financial viability in ways not yet quantifiable.
findings.figures: Not quantified; flagged as active consideration
findings.quote: Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) presents a significant degree of uncertainty and transition risk, which must be actively considered throughout the Council's revenue budget monitoring process. These risks may affect both short-term financial performance and longer-term budget planning.

findings.headline: Multiple income-generating services underachieving budget, with councils proposing fee freezes rather than increases to stimulate demand.
findings.detail: Trade waste income under-recovering by £70k due to post-pandemic customer base decline and cost-of-living pressures. Garden waste income also falling with uptake down over 12-18 months. Car parking at Hook Road shows £30k adverse variance. Meals from Home service continues losing demand to competition. For 2026/27, the council proposes fee freezes for trade waste and garden waste, with a 'marketing campaign' approach rather than price increases.
findings.matters: Structural weakness in revenue streams, combined with councils unable to recover through price, signals persistent demand weakness and constrained pricing power.
findings.figures: Trade waste under-recovery £70k; car parking £30k adverse; garden waste uptake declining over 12-18 months
findings.quote: The customer base has declined since the pandemic and the cost-of-living crisis, as businesses continue to face financial pressures. Garden waste income is also forecast to underachieve, as the service has seen a decline in the uptake over the past 12 -18 months. To try to reinvigorate these services, officers hav e proposed freezes to our 2026/27 trade waste and garden waste fees, with that action to form the basis of marketing campaigns.

findings.headline: Housing homelessness placements generating £1.175m overspend with structural cost increases now embedded in 2026/27 budget.
findings.detail: The council maintains an average of 116-118 net placements in nightly paid accommodation, creating a £1.175m adverse variance in 2025/26. This is not temporary: the 2026/27 budget includes a net increase of £750,000 for nightly paid accommodation costs to create a 'more sustainable approach.' The Section 151 Officer explicitly states this 'ongoing increase in temporary accommodation placements continues to place pressure on the Council's financial and operational resources.'
findings.matters: This is a structural, not cyclical, pressure consuming permanent increases in budget allocation, suggesting either persistent housing shortage or policy shifts that increase council responsibility.
findings.figures: £1.175m Q3 adverse variance; 116-118 net placements; £750,000 budget increase for 2026/27
findings.quote: The ongoing increase in temporary accommodation placements continues to place pressure on the Council's financial and operational resources. While this presents challenges for service delivery and the longer‑term budget position, significant investment has been built into the 2026/27 budget to support a more sustainable approach going forward.

findings.headline: £520,000 deficit forecast at Q3 requires drawdown from Corporate Projects reserve, leaving General Fund at only £55k above minimum.
findings.detail: The Council's £10.269m budget is forecast to outturn at £10.789m. The deficit will be funded from the Corporate Projects reserve, reducing it from £2.630m to £2.110m. The General Fund working balance stands at £1.555m, only £55,000 above the £1.5m minimum balance approved by Council in July 2025.
findings.matters: The council is consuming reserves to fund current operations and has minimal buffer above its minimum reserve level, limiting flexibility to absorb unexpected pressures.
findings.figures: £520,000 deficit; General Fund £1.555m (£55k above minimum); Corporate Projects reserve forecast to £2.110m
findings.quote: The £520,000 projected budget deficit across services for 2025/26 would require a contribution from reserves. The General Fund reserve currently stands at £1.555m, only £55,000 above the £1.5m minimum balance approved by Council in July 2025.
