findings.paper_title: Treasury Management and Investment Strategy 2026/27 Appendix 1
findings.headline: Bank Rate forecast to fall from 4% to 3.25% by Q4 2026, with PWLB rates expected to follow
findings.detail: MUFG forecasts (dated 22 December 2025) expect Bank Rate to fall to 3.75% (already cut to this level by 18 Dec), then to 3.5% in Q2 2026 and 3.25% in Q4 2026. Correspondingly, PWLB certainty rates are expected to fall from current 4.81% (5-year) and 5.39% (10-year) to 4.10% and 4.70% respectively by end-Q4 2027.
findings.matters: Falling borrowing costs may make refinancing of existing debt or funding of capital programmes more economical, though forecast includes significant downside risks from wage growth, geopolitical factors, and fiscal policy.
findings.figures: Current (22 Dec 2025): 5-year PWLB 4.81%, 10-year 5.39%; Target (end-Q4 2027): 5-year 4.10%, 10-year 4.70%; Bank Rate current 3.75%, forecast 3.25% Q4 2026
findings.quote: Our long-term (beyond 10 years) forecast for the neutral level of Bank Rate remains at 3.5%. As all PWLB certainty rates are still above this level, borrowing strategies will need to be reviewed in that context.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management and Investment Strategy 2026/27 Appendix 1
findings.headline: Council maintaining under-borrowed position with £18.4m gap between borrowing need and debt held
findings.detail: As at 31 December 2025, the Capital Financing Requirement (borrowing need) stands at £83.4m but external borrowing is only £64.4m. The council is deliberately using cash reserves as a temporary measure to avoid borrowing, with the position forecast to continue through 2026/27.
findings.matters: Demonstrates disciplined treasury management but reveals reliance on declining cash reserves (forecast to fall to £6m by 2028/29) to cover borrowing needs, creating potential refinancing pressure.
findings.figures: CFR 31 Dec 2025: £83,416k; External Borrowing 31 Dec 2025: £64,427k; Under-borrowing: £18,989k (equivalent to 22.8% of CFR)
findings.quote: The Council is currently maintaining an under-borrowed position. This means that the capital borrowing need (the Capital Financing Requirement) has not been fully funded with loan debt and the Council's cash balances have been used instead as a temporary measure.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management and Investment Strategy 2026/27 Appendix 1
findings.headline: Authorised borrowing limit reduced 37% from £148m to £93m, effective 2026/27
findings.detail: The full Council is being asked to approve a step-change reduction in the Authorised Limit (the legal ceiling for external debt) from £148m in 2024/25-2025/26 to £93m from 2026/27 onwards. This reflects the anticipated legal and structural position following absorption into the new unitary authority.
findings.matters: Signals the anticipated debt position of the successor authority post-reorganisation, constraining future borrowing capacity and potentially requiring debt reduction or refinancing arrangements.
findings.figures: Authorised Limit 2024/25-2025/26: £145m debt + £3m other liabilities = £148m; 2026/27 onwards: £90m debt + £3m other liabilities = £93m
findings.quote: The Council is asked to approve the following Authorised Limit: 2024/25 Estimate 145,000 / 2025/26 Estimate 145,000 / 2026/27 Estimate 90,000 / 2027/28 Estimate 90,000

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management and Investment Strategy 2026/27 Appendix 1
findings.headline: Expected investment balances to fall 75% between 2025/26 and 2028/29
findings.detail: The council's forecast investment balances decline from £24.4m to £6.0m over three years. Core funds (reserves, receipts, CIL, S106) decline by 50% from £30.8m to £15.4m. This reflects both capital spending (including a one-off £3.1m Strategic CIL scheme in 2026/27) and under-borrowing strategy using internal funds.
findings.matters: Shows tightening cash position during institutional transition, potentially limiting operational flexibility and indicating dependence on steady cash generation to meet forecast commitments.
findings.quote: Expected investments 32,601 24,388 15,408 7,821 6,027

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management and Investment Strategy 2026/27 Appendix 1
findings.headline: Commercial property investment programme terminated due to local government reorganisation
findings.detail: The council has ceased all plans for further property purchases under the Commercial Property Acquisition Fund, a programme authorized at £80m in February 2017. This termination is explicitly due to the council's replacement by the new East Surrey unitary authority following reorganisation announced 28 October 2025.
findings.matters: Ends a decade-long income-generation strategy that supported the council's revenue budget, signalling significant strategic pivot during institutional transition and affecting the borrowing need and cash flow forecasts.
findings.figures: Commercial property fund capital expenditure: £0 across 2026/27-2028/29 (previously authorized to £80m)
findings.quote: The future capital programme no longer includes an assumption of additional investment property purchases, funded by borrowing, under the Commercial Property Fund. This is as a result of Local Government Reorganisation which sees Epsom & Ewell Borough Council being replaced by a new unitary authority, East Surrey.

findings.headline: Commercial property acquisition programme halted due to local government reorganisation
findings.detail: The council had approved an £80m commercial property acquisition programme in February 2017, with £30.4m spent to date funded by a combination of external and internal borrowing. The council is now halting all new acquisitions because a new unitary authority will be created in May 2026 with its own property strategy.
findings.matters: This is a material shift in capital strategy affecting future borrowing requirements and represents a significant departure from the prior assumption that the programme would continue to completion.
findings.figures: £80 million approved (February 2017), £30.4 million purchased to date, funded by combination of external and internal borrowing
findings.quote: In light of, this, no new acquisitions are being pursued, and therefore the Treasury Management and Investment Strategy for 2026/27 reflects that position.

findings.headline: Council building Interest Equalisation Reserve to absorb declining investment returns
findings.detail: The council plans to place all £100,000 of mid-year interest overachievement into an Interest Equalisation Reserve (current balance £933,745) to 'help smooth interest returns in future years'. This is an explicit acknowledgment that income volatility is expected.
findings.matters: Building a reserve to cushion income decline shows the council recognises the problem is structural. A lender should assess whether this reserve is adequate, or whether service savings will be required instead.
findings.figures: Interest Equalisation Reserve £933,745 currently, with planned addition of £100,000
findings.quote: any additional interest generated in 2025/26 will be set-aside in an earmarked Interest Equalisation Reserve to help smooth interest returns in future years

findings.headline: Section 151 Officer warns reserves will continue to diminish if budget strategy not progressed and cost reduction targets not achieved
findings.detail: The council's Section 151 Officer explicitly warns that failure to progress the budget strategy and achieve significant net cost reduction could lead to continuing reserve diminution and eventually render the council unable to set a balanced budget.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion is a leading indicator of financial distress; inability to set a balanced budget could trigger regulatory intervention and affect the council's creditworthiness.
findings.figures: None specified
findings.quote: Should the Council not progress the proposed budget strategy and fail to achieve a significant net reduction in its cost of services, there is a clear risk that reserves will continue to diminish with the Council eventually becoming unable to set a balanced budget

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation service requires an additional £500,000 funding to address a structural deficit, while a previously planned £300,000 saving has been removed.
findings.detail: The medium term financial strategy was updated to allocate an additional £500,000 to address a current adverse position in temporary accommodation identified in quarter 1 revenue monitoring. A previously agreed £300,000 saving within this service for 2026/27 has also been removed from the plan.
findings.matters: A structural deficit in a statutory homelessness service signals growing demand or cost pressures the council cannot manage within existing budgets.
findings.figures: £500,000 additional funding; £300,000 previously agreed saving removed
findings.quote: The additional £500,000 within the temporary accommodation budget aims to address the current adverse position forecast at the quarter 1 revenue budget monitoring stage

findings.headline: Council faces a growing budget deficit of £1.93 million in 2026/27, rising to £5.06 million by 2028/29.
findings.detail: The Strategy and Resources Committee agreed budget targets on 15 July 2025 in response to a projected deficit that will nearly triple within three years. This requires significant cost reduction across the council to maintain a balanced budget.
findings.matters: A growing, multi-year deficit signals deteriorating financial sustainability and would directly influence lending decisions and the council's financial stability.
findings.figures: £1.93 million deficit in 2026/27, rising to £5.06 million by 2028/29
findings.quote: latest forecasts show that the Council faces a projected budget deficit of £1.93 million in 2026/27, rising to £5.06 million by 2028/29

findings.headline: 2026/27 staffing budget increase of 3% is provisional pending completion of pay negotiations still underway
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget assumes a 3% increase in staffing budgets, explicitly noted as 'for EWDC planning purposes only while pay deal negotiations for 2026/27 remain ongoing'. The final staffing budget will not be confirmed until pay deals conclude.
findings.matters: If pay settlements exceed the 3% assumption, staffing costs will overrun unless other budget reductions offset the overspend
findings.figures: 3% provisional staffing increase
findings.quote: Staffing budgets have been increased by an indicative 3%, although this is for EWDC planning purposes only while pay deal negotiations for 2026/27 remain ongoing.

findings.headline: 2026/27 budget increases of 3% fall short of current inflation of 3.8%
findings.detail: The budget applies 3% inflation to most running budgets, staffing, and fees and charges. However, current inflation (August 2025 CPI) stands at 3.8%, creating a 0.8 percentage-point shortfall. The report acknowledges inflation is forecast to decrease but provides no detail on timing or magnitude.
findings.matters: A budget increase below current inflation signals that costs may outpace provision; mid-year budget pressures could emerge if inflation remains elevated
findings.figures: Inflation 3.8% (August 2025 CPI); budget increase 3%; inflation shortfall 0.8 percentage points
findings.quote: Inflation is currently at 3.8% (August 2025) consumer price index although inflation is forecast to decrease later in the year. The Government's current inflation target is 2%

findings.headline: 2026/27 budget requires 3% precept increase to balance, with contribution to working balance rising from £7,599 to £13,743
findings.detail: The indicative 2026/27 budget cannot be balanced without a 3% precept increase from all three funding sources: Epsom and Ewell Borough Council (60%), Epsom Racecourse (30%), and the Training Board (10%). The Borough Council's share of the precept increase therefore rises as the overall budget pressure increases.
findings.matters: Borough Council contributes 60% of this precept; precept increases indicate budget pressures and rising contingent funding demands on the council
findings.figures: 3% precept increase; contribution to working balance £13,743 (up from £7,599 in 2025/26)
findings.quote: Based on the indicative budget, an overall 3% increase in precepts would be required to set a balanced budget for next year.

findings.headline: Council imposing freeze on new revenue growth items, requiring them to be fully funded from existing budgets
findings.detail: Any additional new revenue growth items (service enhancements) supported by policy committees must be fully funded from existing budgets. This reflects the severity of the deficit and represents a hardening constraint on new spending.
findings.matters: This signals financial stress and a tightening of spending discipline; it indicates the council sees the deficit as serious enough to prevent new commitments.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: for any additional new revenue growth items (i.e. service enhancements resulting in increased net expenditure) supported by policy committees, the committee or Council will need to identify how these can be fully funded from existing budgets.

findings.headline: Council's financial forecasts made amid uncertainty from Local Government Reorganisation proposals with outcome expected October 2025
findings.detail: Epsom and Ewell submitted a unitary authority proposal following the December 2024 English Devolution White Paper. The outcome of the reorganisation was expected in October 2025. The council is required to set budgets that are sustainable and prudent pending this outcome.
findings.matters: Lenders need visibility on structural uncertainty that could materially change the council's future viability, funding, and financial obligations.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: It is important to note that these forecasts are made at a time of uncertainty in local government finance, particularly in Surrey as it responds to the Local Government Reorganisation. Following the December 2024 English Devolution White Paper, council has submitted its unitary proposal and awaits the outcome which is expected in October.

findings.headline: Section 151 Officer warns reserves will diminish without significant net reductions in service costs, risking inability to set balanced budget
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer explicitly warns that without progress on the budget strategy and without achieving significant net reductions in service costs, reserves will continue to diminish. The council could eventually become unable to set a balanced budget.
findings.matters: Lenders assess reserve adequacy as a critical indicator of financial health; ongoing depletion signals distress and potential inability to absorb shocks.
findings.figures: None specified
findings.quote: Should the Council not progress the proposed budget strategy and fail to achieve a significant net reduction in its cost of services, there is a clear risk that reserves will continue to diminish with the Council eventually becoming unable to set a balanced budget.

findings.headline: Epsom and Ewell faces a projected budget deficit of £1.93 million in 2026/27, widening to £5.06 million by 2028/29
findings.detail: Strategy & Resources Committee agreed on budget targets in July 2025 to address this deficit through multiple workstreams: asset utilisation reviews, fees and charges review (CPI + 1%), reserve reviews, and external funding opportunities. The deficits show the council's expenditure exceeds its baseline income.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council can close a deficit of this scale through its planned savings, and what happens to reserves if it cannot.
findings.figures: £1.93 million in 2026/27, £5.06 million by 2028/29
findings.quote: The committee noted that for financial planning purposes, latest forecasts show that the Council faces a projected budget deficit of £1.93 million in 2026/27, rising to £5.06 million by 2028/29.

findings.headline: The Council's debt servicing depends entirely on rental and capital income from its property investment company, not the operating budget.
findings.detail: The Council reports that its net financing costs are fully covered by income from its own investment property acquisitions and the Epsom & Ewell Property Investment Company. This means the general fund does not fund debt servicing costs, but creates a dependency on property market performance.
findings.matters: Concentration of debt servicing on property investment income creates vulnerability to changes in rental income, property valuations, or tenant default, which would directly impact the council's ability to meet borrowing obligations.
findings.figures: Financing costs fully funded by property acquisition income; ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream -1%
findings.quote: In practice, the financing costs are fully funded by further income generated from both the Council's and Epsom & Ewell Property Investment Company's investment property acquisitions.

findings.headline: Investment balances fell by £1.3m as the Council's available cash declined.
findings.detail: Investments at 31 March fell from £23.2m in 2023/24 to £21.9m in 2024/25. The Council explicitly attributes this to lower cash balances, which also reduced investment income and contributed to the negative financing costs ratio.
findings.matters: Declining cash balances may signal underlying cash flow pressures and reduce the council's financial flexibility and ability to absorb unexpected shocks.
findings.figures: Investments 31 March 2024 £23,200k; 31 March 2025 £21,866k (decrease £1,334k)
findings.quote: Due to the decreased income generated on the Council's investments as a result of lower cash balances, the ratio for 2024/25 is a negative figure

findings.headline: Capital expenditure of £6.0m was only 11% of the £53.1m forecast for 2024/25, driven almost entirely by the unspent commercial property fund.
findings.detail: The Council estimated £53.1m capital spending for 2024/25 but spent only £6.0m. The £47.1m variance is attributable almost entirely to the £49.6m commercial property fund projected to be drawn but not actually borrowed. Other capital programmes were broadly in line with or above forecast.
findings.matters: Large capital plan variances signal weak forecasting capability or unresolved capital project delays, both material to lenders assessing the council's ability to deliver planned capital programmes.
findings.figures: Capital Expenditure: Estimated £53,058k, Actual £6,011k; Unfinanced capex commercial properties: Estimated £49,569k, Actual £0k
findings.quote: For the purposes of forecasting only, the £49.6m balance was projected to be spent in 2024/25, to ensure the prudential indicators reflect previously agreed limits. The Council has not incurred this borrowing

findings.headline: The £49.6m Commercial Property Fund remains unspent after five years with no new property acquisitions since 2020.
findings.detail: The Council agreed to borrow up to £80m in 2016/17 for commercial property acquisitions. It spent £30m on four properties but has not pursued any new acquisitions since 2020, leaving £49.6m of the approved borrowing limit undrawn. The Council states it would only spend this if an updated Property Investment Strategy is agreed and stringent criteria are met.
findings.matters: Indicates the capital investment strategy has stalled or become more risk-averse, creating uncertainty about future capital spending and the underlying assumptions for the original £80m borrowing case.
findings.figures: £49.6m remaining limit, £30m spent on four properties, no acquisitions since 2020
findings.quote: There have been no new acquisitions since 2020.

news_drafts.headline: Epsom and Ewell's three-year funding gap falls from £5.063m to £0.579m, 2026/27 budget balanced
news_drafts.lead:
Epsom and Ewell Borough Council's three-year funding gap has fallen from £5.063m to £0.579m, and its budget for 2026/27 is balanced. The figures are in the external auditors' annual report on value for money for the year ended 31 March 2026, which went to the Audit and Scrutiny Committee on 12 November.

The report attributes the reduction to updated funding assumptions, expenditure reductions and planned efficiencies. It gives no split between the three.

The remaining £0.579m is made up of £0.206m in 2027/28 and £0.373m in 2028/29. According to the report, both residual gaps will transfer to East Surrey Council after vesting day.

news_drafts.headline: Epsom and Ewell reports £250k Q1 overspend on nightly paid housing despite budget for 100 households
news_drafts.lead:
Epsom and Ewell Borough Council is forecasting a £250,000 overspend on housing in the first quarter of 2026/27, after demand for nightly paid accommodation for homeless households rose beyond what it had budgeted for. The council's quarter one budget monitoring report (the in-year check of spending against budget) says the overspend will be covered by corporate contingency, money held centrally for unforeseen costs.

The council had raised its 2026/27 budget to provide for an average of 100 households in nightly paid accommodation. The report says demand "dramatically increased" in the first quarter as landlords responded to the Renters Rights Act, which came into force in May. The overspend sits within a total budget of £11.868m.

The paper says a £750,000 growth budget was put into the nightly paid service for 2026/27 "to address some of the structural deficit in this area". The budget has since been increased by a further £128,500 in the year, funded from the council's inflationary provision. The council's chief finance officer (the section 151 officer, who has a legal duty to warn if the council cannot balance its books) describes the position as "highly sensitive to fluctuations in demand, availability of accommodation and wider housing market conditions."

news_drafts.headline: Epsom and Ewell halts capital investment following government reorganization announcement
news_drafts.lead: Epsom and Ewell council has ceased acquisitions under its Commercial Property Investment Fund following the government's 28 October announcement that Surrey's current county, district and borough councils will be replaced by two unitary authorities. The council had estimated £49.6m capital expenditure on commercial properties for 2025/26 but made no property purchases, spending £2.8m against a total capital forecast of £58.3m. Meanwhile, the council's treasury performance improved: net investment income reached £1,178,313, exceeding its mid-year forecast by £236,313 despite lower average cash balances and declining interest rates. The council's average net return on investments was 4.23%, outperforming the SONIA benchmark. The council maintained its Public Works Loan Board debt flat at £64.4m and required no temporary borrowing during the year.
